title: Chinese and Japanese text, and characters outside the BMP

cases.note: LEN counts characters: two Chinese characters are 2.
LENB counts 2 bytes per CJK character only when a double-byte language is the default editing language; otherwise it equals LEN. Locale trap.
FIND counts characters; FINDB counts bytes under a double-byte language.
LEFTB with an odd byte count cuts a double-byte character in half; what is returned in its place?
MID on mixed kanji and kana counts characters.
UPPER also upper-cases full-width Latin letters.
ASC turns full-width into half-width and DBCS the other way, but only under a double-byte language.
CODE returns a code in the Windows ANSI code page (936 for Chinese), so the result depends on the machine.
UNICODE and UNICHAR use code points and do not depend on the locale.
Excel counts UTF-16 code units: one emoji is LEN 2. UNICODE still returns the full code point.
LEFT of an emoji by 1 returns half a surrogate pair (written as \ud83d in the JSON).
EXACT tells full-width a from a; does = treat them as equal too?
Does SEARCH ignore character width as well as case?
SUBSTITUTE removes a CJK character.
REPT repeats CJK text.
[DBNum1] and [DBNum2] write numbers with Chinese numerals; the exact output depends on the locale.
NUMBERSTRING exists only in Chinese Excel; elsewhere #NAME?.
TRIM removes only the ASCII space; the ideographic space U+3000 stays.
Half-width ｶﾞ is two characters (ka + voiced mark); ASC of full-width ガ gives that pair under a double-byte language.
The order of CJK text in comparisons follows the collation of the locale.
Exact MATCH on CJK text.
LEN and LENB of a cell holding CJK text.
PROPER capitalises letters after any non-letter, including after CJK characters.
COUNTIF wildcards count characters, not bytes.
